What Texas law says about recording

  • Office: County Clerk.
  • Address: Deed Records are handled at the Paul Elizondo Tower, San Antonio.

Bexar County by the numbers

Which Bexar County office records deeds and liens?

The Bexar County Clerk's Recordings Division files and maintains real property records, personal property records, notices of trustee sale and public notices. Filing in person happens at the Paul Elizondo Tower, 101 W. Nueva, Suite 103, San Antonio 78205, phone 210-335-2581. A Southside Annex inside Precinct 1 at 3505 Pleasanton Rd. also takes filings, at 210-335-3522.

The doors are open weekdays from 8 a.m., closing at 5 p.m. except Wednesdays, when the office stays open until 5:45. Deed Records, the desk that pulls copies and researches liens, is in Suite B109 of the same tower at 210-335-2273. Mail goes to the Clerk's Office, Attn: Recordings, 100 Dolorosa, Suite 104, San Antonio.

The clerk's site lists a "Records on the Run" satellite office that rotates through precinct offices and community centers each month, so a filer can skip the downtown trip. The clerk also runs a Vanguard Property Alert that warns owners about potentially fraudulent filings, and accepts wills for safekeeping.

What are Bexar County's fees for filing a deed?

Filing a one-page instrument with the Bexar County Clerk costs $25.00, and every added page is $4.00. The first-page charge breaks into a $5.00 recording fee, a $10.00 records archive fee and a $10.00 records management fee, all effective January 1, 2024.

Source: Bexar County Clerk, Real Property Recording Fees, which lists every total from 1 through 50 pages.

The same page lists the add-ons you are most likely to meet:

  • Notice of trustee sale: $2.00 filing, $1.00 for a plain copy
  • Federal tax lien instruments: $30.00 total
  • Plats: $81.00 total per mylar
  • Deed copies: $1.00 per page plus $5.00 per certification
  • Electronic copy of an electronic document: $1.00 up to 10 pages, then $0.10 per page

What are the filing rules for Bexar County recordings?

The clerk records only originals with original signatures and will not record a copy. Documents are cashiered, given an instrument number and scanned on the spot, then the originals are handed back or returned. Payment can be cash, credit card, check or money order, with checks written to the Bexar County Clerk.

Electronic filing is a separate lane. Section 195.003 of the Local Government Code limits it to attorneys, banks and credit unions, federally backed mortgage lenders, persons approved to make regulated loans, title companies, state agencies and municipal clerks. The clerk lists six approved e-filing providers, among them CSC, Simplifile, ePN, Indecomm and Hopdox.

The clerk's staff do not draft deeds and do not vouch for a clear title, and they send people who want assurance to title companies and attorneys. A conveyance also has to be signed and acknowledged before a notary or similar officer before it can go on record, a rule the Texas county clerk manual ties to Property Code 12.001(b).

How can a seller check for liens on a Bexar County house?

Start with the clerk's public records search, or visit the Deed Records Department in Suite B109 of the Paul Elizondo Tower, where staff can point you to recorded liens against a property. The clerk does not guarantee clear title and takes no responsibility for encumbrances, so a guaranteed search comes from a title company, with an attorney as the other route.

Mortgage foreclosure notices can be pulled from the same search. A list is also available through the clerk's GIS Foreclosure Map or at the Deed Records counter, while the list of tax foreclosures comes from the law firm that handles them at 210-225-4422.

  • Release of lien: record the original in person at the tower or mail it to the courthouse office, at $25.00 for the first page
  • Lost deed: a certified copy runs $1.00 per page plus $5.00 per certification
  • Plain copies: found online under Land Records in the Official Public Records Search

How do foreclosure sales work in Bexar County?

Mortgage and tax foreclosure sales in Bexar County are public cash auctions held the first Tuesday of each month between 10:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. When that Tuesday falls on January 1 or July 4, the sale moves to Wednesday. Per the clerk, bidding happens outdoors beside the courthouse, in the gap between it and the Paul Elizondo Tower, unless Commissioners Court names a different spot.

Bidders need no registration for a mortgage foreclosure, but registration is required to bid on a tax foreclosure. Only cash or certified funds work, and personal checks are refused. A GIS Foreclosure Map tracks notices and is refreshed twice a month, on the first Friday after the auction and about 18 days before the next sale.

Redemption periods are stated on the clerk's page: two years for agricultural or homestead property and six months for other property, counted from the day the sale deed goes on record. The clerk also hosts a free foreclosure training seminar on the first Tuesday of each month. The State Law Library adds that a notice of sale must be posted and placed on file with the clerk 21 or more days ahead.

How big is Bexar County, and what does its housing look like?

Bexar County spans 1,248 square miles around San Antonio, which serves as both seat and biggest city. The Handbook of Texas places it along the Balcones Escarpment, with hilly Edwards Plateau country in the northwest and flatter prairie and South Texas plains elsewhere. The San Antonio River and the Medina River drain it, and Interstates 10, 35, 37 and 410 plus U.S. 281 and U.S. 90 carry traffic through.

Bexar was established as a county on December 20, 1836. The mission-era area around the Alamo and the five Spanish missions is part of the historic record behind many older lots, and military bases, tourism, medical centers and higher education drive the present economy. Suburbs include Alamo Heights, Converse, Universal City, Terrell Hills and Castle Hills.

  • Mid-2025 estimate: 2,160,088 residents, 7.5 percent above the 2020 base
  • Housing units: 853,619, with owners living in 58.8 percent of occupied homes
  • Typical owned home, 2020 to 2024 survey: valued at $262,200
  • Typical monthly rent: $1,354
  • Density: 1,620.0 residents per square mile

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts page is the source for each of these.

Who values property in Bexar County, and who collects the tax?

Valuation and protests belong to the Bexar Central Appraisal District, and payments go to the Bexar County Tax Assessor-Collector. BCAD's site says it takes no tax payments. It mails value notices to new owners and to anyone whose market value climbed $1,000 or more, and a protest can be filed without a notice.

The clerk's page gives 210-335-6628 for tax certificates and payment questions, at the Vista Verde Plaza Building. Across Texas, value is fixed each January 1, bills arrive in October, and unpaid tax turns delinquent February 1. School districts exempt $140,000 of a homestead, and seniors or disabled owners receive $60,000 on top.

Sellers should watch the lien. Texas attaches the year's tax lien to the land each January 1, which is why a closing agent wants a current tax certificate and proof that earlier years are paid.

More questions about Bexar County, TX Property Records

What is the first-page fee for a Bexar County deed?

It is $25.00 in all: $5.00 for recording, $10.00 for the records archive and $10.00 for records management. Extra pages are $4.00 each.

Will the Bexar County Clerk record a photocopy of my deed?

No. The clerk requires original documents with original signatures and says it will not record a copy.Bring the signed original to the Paul Elizondo Tower or mail it to the courthouse office.

Which day of the month are Bexar County foreclosure auctions?

They happen on the first Tuesday of each month between 10:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. If the first Tuesday is January 1 or July 4, the sale is held on the first Wednesday.

Can I order a certified copy of a Bexar County deed by mail?

Yes. Send the request to the clerk's office in the courthouse, or ask in person at the Deed Records Department in the Paul Elizondo Tower. The price is $1.00 a page and $5.00 for the certification.

Does the Bexar Central Appraisal District collect property tax?

No. BCAD handles values, exemptions and protests only. Tax payments and tax certificates go through the Bexar County Tax Assessor-Collector at 210-335-6628.

Brazoria County by the numbers

Where does Brazoria County keep its deed and lien records?

The Brazoria County Clerk's Recording Department keeps them, in the Administration Building at 237 East Locust, Suite 102, Angleton, TX 77515. The recording and vitals line is 979-864-1059. Angleton is the county seat, and trustee sale notices are posted at the courthouse there.

The clerk's site runs a searchable database of real property records that you can use from home or on public computers at the Angleton office. New users create a login and answer a verification email before searching. The office adds that its clerks are recorders, not qualified examiners of the records, so they will not run a title search for you. The online database is also not the official repository, and some information is redacted as state law requires.

  • Plain copies: $1.00 per page
  • Certified copies: $1.00 per page plus $5.00 per document, mailed by regular post only
  • Copy requests go through an online application, and payment follows an approval email

What does recording a document cost in Brazoria County?

A one-page deed costs $25.00 to record in Brazoria County. That total is a $10.00 records management fee, a $10.00 records archive fee and a $5.00 first-page fee, and each additional page is $4.00. Names indexed beyond the first five add $0.25 each.

Document or serviceBrazoria County fee
First page of a recorded instrument$25.00

Source: Brazoria County Clerk, Recording and Vitals Fees.

Penalties catch careless filers. A deed with no grantee mailing address owes the greater of $25 or twice the filing fee on top of normal charges. The fee for a page doubles if names are not typed or printed under each signature, and doubles again for a page lacking a heading that identifies the document type.

What formatting rules does the Brazoria County Clerk enforce?

The county clerk publishes a long checklist, and a deed that misses a line can be rejected. Since January 1, 2026, anyone presenting a real property document in person must show photo ID to the clerk, under Local Government Code 191.010.

  • Original signatures, with each signer's name printed or typed beneath, and a notary acknowledgment with a clear, dark seal
  • English language, or a certified translation attached
  • White paper between 8.5 x 11 and 8.5 x 14 inches, with type of at least 8 point in black or blue ink
  • A 3 inch top margin on page one and a heading naming the document type
  • A legal description showing the property lies in Brazoria County, or a reference to a prior recording that does
  • The Notice of Confidentiality Rights in 12 point bold type or 12 point capitals on any transfer to or from an individual

The county page also explains Senate Bill 30, effective September 1, 2021, which gives an owner a court process to have discriminatory restrictions in old records reviewed, with no filing fee under the statute.

E-recording is open only to filers qualified under Local Government Code 195.003, through Simplifile, CSC/Ingeo, Nationwide Title Clearing, ePN, Indecomm or hopdox. Re-recording an e-recorded deed requires a certified copy or the original with the first and last pages of the e-recorded version attached.

What other services does the Brazoria County Clerk price?

The fee page lists several mail and data services beyond a basic recording. Expedited service is $5.00 plus the mail option you choose, which is $5.00 for 3 day priority post or $30.00 for FedEx overnight. Title plants that want bulk data can buy daily, weekly or two week CDs of images and indices at $6.00, $8.00 and $12.00, or daily and weekly FTP at $3.00 and $5.00.

Faxed pages cost $1.00 each plus a usage charge of $1.00 in the calling area or $2.00 outside it, and the clerk says vital records cannot be faxed. Copies of 11 x 17 pages are $2.00 each, and a 24 x 36 plat or map copy is $5.00 a page.

What is Brazoria County like, and how does the land affect records?

Brazoria County is a 1,407 square mile Gulf Coast county at the mouth of the Brazos River, and flood and hurricane exposure shapes how its land is held and insured. The Handbook of Texas notes 52 inches of annual rainfall, a long list of historic hurricanes and floods, and soils that are productive when well drained.

The county was created in 1836, and Angleton replaced the town of Brazoria as seat in 1896. Pearland is the largest city, and Brazosport is a community of nine cities that includes Lake Jackson, Clute, Freeport and Surfside Beach. State highways 6, 35, 36 and 288 serve the area. The economy leans on petrochemicals, with Dow Chemical arriving at Freeport in 1939, plus agriculture, fishing and tourism.

Census figures show a fast-growing, higher income market:

  • Population estimate for July 1, 2025: 419,080, up 12.6 percent from April 2020
  • Housing units: 162,298, with 74.1 percent owner occupied
  • Median value of owner occupied homes, 2020 to 2024: $301,600
  • Median household income: $97,993, and mean commute 30.6 minutes
  • Median gross rent: $1,454

How does the appraisal district fit in for Brazoria County owners?

The Brazoria Central Appraisal District, at 500 North Chenango in Angleton, sets the value and handles exemptions, while the clerk records the deed. Its home page reminds owners that notices of appraised value are due by April 1 for single-family homes and May 1 for other property, or as soon after as practical.

The district also describes a homestead audit program under Senate Bill 1801, which requires each residence homestead exemption to be reviewed at least once every five tax years. Owners who get no letter need not file again. The Tax Assessor-Collector's office, at 111 E. Locust in Angleton, is listed at 979-864-1320 for tax bills.

On the state side, the school district homestead exemption is $140,000, and owners 65 or older or disabled receive $60,000 more. A tax lien attaches every January 1, and delinquent taxes after January 31 carry penalty and interest. When a house is sold, the recorded deed is what moves ownership on the appraisal rolls, so file it promptly after closing.

What recording problems slow a Brazoria County sale?

The usual culprits are missing notary details, a legal description that does not match the prior deed, and unreleased liens. A release of a paid-off lien is itself a recordable instrument, so ask the lender for it in writing and confirm it appears in the clerk's index.

Inherited houses need extra proof. The State Law Library says an affidavit of heirship is a sworn, court-unverified statement filed with the county clerk, and no law forces third parties to accept it. An order from the probate court, or a transfer on death deed recorded before the owner's death, gives a buyer firmer footing.

Foreclosure timing also shows up in these records. A notice of sale must be posted at the courthouse and filed with the clerk at least 21 days before the first-Tuesday auction, and Brazoria County charges $8.00 for a trustee notice.

What is the first-page recording fee in Brazoria County?

It is $25.00 in total, made of a $10.00 records management fee, a $10.00 records archive fee and a $5.00 first-page fee. Each additional page costs $4.00.

Do I need photo ID to record a deed in Brazoria County?

Yes, for in-person filings. Since January 1, 2026 anyone presenting a document for the real property records must provide photo ID to the clerk, per Local Government Code 191.010.

Can Brazoria County staff search the records for me?

No. The clerks are recorders and are not qualified examiners, so you search the online database yourself or use the public computers at 237 East Locust in Angleton.

How do I get a certified copy of a Brazoria County deed?

Search the database for the document number and page count, then submit the online copy application. Certified copies cost $1.00 per page plus $5.00 per document and are sent by regular mail.

What happens if my deed has no grantee mailing address?

The clerk adds a penalty fee. Texas Property Code 11.003 sets it at the greater of $25 or twice the statutory filing fee, charged on top of the regular recording cost.

Cameron County by the numbers

Where do I search Cameron County property records?

Start with the Official Public Records search linked from the Cameron County Clerk's page, then call the Brownsville main office at (956) 544-0815 about anything the search does not show. The clerk's Recordings Division files and keeps real property records, personal property records, notices of trustee sales and public notices. Records that no law or court order restricts are open through the Public Records Search.

The clerk's public access portals page lists separate databases for foreclosure sales, official records, official records from 1848 to 1912, and judicial records. A very old instrument belongs in the 1848 to 1912 portal, so check there before you decide a record is missing.

Which Cameron County Clerk office should I visit?

Go to the Brownsville main office at 835 East Levee Street, 3rd Floor, for deeds and liens. The clerk lists four more locations, and the one nearest your house may save a trip.

Cameron County Clerk locations, as listed on the clerk's own page

  • Recording hours on the land records page run from 8 in the morning to 4 in the afternoon on weekdays.
  • The La Feria annex is open on Tuesdays and Thursdays only, from 8 until 4:30.
  • Older civil, probate and deed volumes are stored at the records management facility in the San Benito annex building.

How do I record a deed in Cameron County?

Bring the original deed with original signatures, because the clerk will not record a copy. File it at the Brownsville office or any satellite office, or mail it to the Filing and Recording Department, P.O. Box 2178, Brownsville, TX 78522.

The clerk says recordings are completed as they arrive. Once a document is cashiered, given an instrument number and scanned, the original goes back to the filer. Electronic filing runs through the e-recording companies the clerk names, and the page limits it to groups such as Texas attorneys, banks, credit unions and title insurance companies or agents.

Two state rules decide whether the clerk can accept your deed. It has to be acknowledged before a notary or another authorized officer, or sworn before two witnesses, under Property Code 12.001(b). And a missing grantee mailing address can add a $25 charge, according to the Texas county clerk manual.

On price, the clerk's land records page prints $35 for the first page and $4 for each added page, in its paragraph on recording a release of lien. The state manual lists a $5 first page and $4 for each added page as the base recording fee, before add-on records fees. Ask the clerk which total applies to your deed before you mail a check, and make it payable to the Cameron County Clerk.

How do I get a copy of a recorded deed or check for liens?

Use the Official Public Records Search, choose Property Records, and pull a plain or certified copy there. You can also email officialpublicrecords@co.cameron.tx.us. For a certified copy by mail, write to the County Clerk's Office, P.O. Box 2178, Brownsville, TX 78522-2178. The printed charge is $1 per page, $5 per certification and $5 per search.

Liens recorded against a property show up in the same search. The clerk states that its office does not guarantee a clear title and is not responsible for encumbrances, and it points owners to title companies and attorneys. For a sale, the title company will look for:

  • Deeds of trust and the releases that should follow a payoff
  • Tax liens and judgments filed against the owner
  • Probate filings when an owner has died
  • Gaps in the chain of deeds, such as a missing heir's signature

Does the Cameron Appraisal District keep deeds or tax bills?

No. The Cameron Appraisal District sets values and administers exemptions, and its own site sends deed copy and subdivision plat requests to the county clerk. It also says it does not collect taxes or hold tax amounts.

The district notes that people often mistake it for the Cameron County Tax Office, which sits across U.S. Highway 83 at 1390 W Expressway 83 in San Benito. The district opens at 7:30 and closes at 5:30 from Monday through Thursday, and keeps 8 to 5 on Fridays. Property Search and Map Search are linked from its home page.

The Texas Comptroller calendar fixes value and ownership as of January 1. Owners can protest by May 15 or the 30th day after the appraisal notice, whichever is later, and the payment page says a bill unpaid on February 1 turns delinquent. School districts must give a $140,000 homestead exemption, and the application goes to the appraisal district.

What if a Cameron County owner died and the title is unclear?

A probate filing usually clears it. The clerk's Probate Department, at 974 East Harrison Street, 2nd Floor, Brownsville, handles probate of a will and issuance of letters testamentary, probate of a will as a muniment of title, letters of administration and determination of heirship.

The department also describes a small estate affidavit. By the clerk's description it applies when there is no will, the estate is under $75,000 and no real estate is involved. A house therefore needs one of the other routes. Call (956) 544-0826 for forms, and ask the clerk for the 2026 probate fee schedule that the department page links.

What do the Census figures say about Cameron County housing?

The county covers a large area and holds a few hundred thousand people. These figures come from Census QuickFacts:

  • Population: 433,946 in the July 2025 estimate, up from 421,017 at the 2020 census
  • Land area: 891.71 square miles, about 472 people per square mile in 2020
  • Housing units: 166,569 in July 2025, with 2,702 building permits in 2025
  • Owner-occupied rate: 65.2%, and 138,433 households
  • Home value reported by owners, middle figure: $136,500 (2020 to 2024)
  • Middle gross rent: $912, and middle household income: $52,601

These are county-wide medians. A house in Brownsville, Harlingen or San Benito can sit far above or below them, so use the figures as background only.

When and where are Cameron County foreclosure sales held?

The clerk's page says the sale runs on the first Tuesday of every month between 10:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m., on the west side of the Cameron County Courthouse or at another spot the Commissioners Court designates. The sale is open to the public for bidding, and the notices are filed with the clerk's Recordings Division.

The same page prints redemption periods: two years for agricultural-use or homestead property and six months for all other property, counted from the date the deed is recorded. Questions about tax certificates go to the Tax Assessor-Collector at 956-544-0800. If your house has a notice of sale on file, tell a title company early, because it affects what can still be recorded and sold.

More questions about Cameron County, TX Property Records

Where is the Cameron County Clerk's main office?

It is at 835 East Levee Street, 3rd Floor, Brownsville, TX 78520, and the phone is (956) 544-0815. The clerk also lists offices in San Benito, Harlingen and La Feria, plus a courthouse location at 974 E. Harrison Street.

Will the Cameron County Clerk record a photocopy of my deed?

No. The clerk's land records page says the original documents with original signatures are required and that the office will not record a copy. After scanning, the original is returned to the filer.

What does a certified copy of a deed cost in Cameron County?

By mail, the clerk prints $1 per page, $5 per certification and $5 per search. Plain and certified copies can also be requested through the Official Public Records Search under Property Records.

Can the Cameron Appraisal District give me a copy of my deed?

No. The district's site says it does not give out copies of deeds or subdivision plats and refers those requests to the Cameron County Clerk's office. Call the clerk at (956) 544-0815.

How can I tell if my Cameron County house is facing a foreclosure sale?

Search the clerk's foreclosure sales portal and the Official Public Records for a notice of trustee sale. Sales take place on the first Tuesday of each month, so a notice on file points to the next first Tuesday. A title company can confirm the status.

Bell County by the numbers

Where do I search and record property records in Bell County?

Deeds, liens and plats for Bell County are filed with the County Clerk in Belton, and the Property Records/Recordings desk answers at (254) 933-5171. The clerk works from the Bell County Justice Center at 1201 Huey Road, Belton, TX 76513, weekdays from 8 in the morning to 5 in the afternoon, and takes mail at P.O. Box 480 in Belton.

The clerk's real estate page says the Official Public Records are searchable online, and the main clerk page also links a SUPERSEARCH tool that uses OCR plus a CountyFusion search. A Property Fraud Alert sign-up sits on the same page, which is worth a few minutes if you own a house you rarely visit.

Plan around the cutoff. The clerk takes no daily business transactions after 4:30 p.m., and the cutoff moves to 4:15 p.m. on the last business day of the month. If you are closing on a month-end Friday, get the signed original to the title company early.

  • Recording desk: (254) 933-5171, with an email address listed for deed recordings on the clerk's page
  • Civil and probate records: (254) 933-5174
  • Plats: an alphabetical and numerical directory on the clerk's site

What will Bell County charge to file a deed?

Filing a single-page deed in Bell County costs $10.00, made up of a $5.00 filing fee and a $5.00 records management fee. Each added page that carries visible marks is $4.00, and the clerk adds $0.25 for each grantor or grantee indexed past the first five. The schedule below is the clerk's own, listed as effective January 1, 2024 after Senate Bill 1612.

The clerk also prints a page-count chart. These totals come straight from it:

  • 1 page: $10.00
  • 5 pages: $26.00
  • 10 pages: $46.00
  • 25 pages: $106.00
  • 50 pages: $206.00

The office states it cannot hold or record an instrument without the proper fee, and it does not accept personal out-of-state checks.

What must a document show before the Bell County Clerk accepts it?

It must be an original, notarized document or a certified copy of the original. The clerk's page also asks filers to leave a 2 inch margin for the recording stamp and instrument number.

State law backs up the notary step. A conveyance of real property can be recorded only if it is signed and acknowledged, or sworn to, before an authorized officer, according to the Texas county clerk manual. The same manual says a deed that leaves out a grantee's mailing address can pick up an extra $25 charge, so check that line before you sign.

Electronic filing is limited to the entities named in Local Government Code 195.003, such as attorneys, banks and title companies. Bell County lists these e-recording vendors: CSC, EPN eRecording Network, Simplifile, Hopdox and Indecomm Global Services. A homeowner mailing a deed to the clerk, by contrast, sends the paper original.

How is Bell County laid out, and what does that mean for a records search?

Bell County is a 1,055 square mile county in east central Texas, roughly 45 miles north of Austin, and its records cover very different kinds of land. The Handbook of Texas describes the Balcones Escarpment running through the middle, with level Blackland Prairie farmland to the east and rolling Grand Prairie uplands to the west.

The county was formed in 1850 and its seat, first called Nolanville, took the name Belton in 1851. Today Killeen is the largest city, and Temple grew up around the Santa Fe railroad headquarters in 1881. Other towns include Harker Heights, Nolanville, Salado and Morgan's Point Resort. Interstate 35 and U.S. 190 are the main roads, and Belton Lake and Stillhouse Hollow Lake shape the lakeside lots.

That mix produces the paperwork variety a title searcher sees here: old farm tracts with metes and bounds descriptions, subdivision plats around Killeen and Temple, lakefront parcels, and homes near Fort Cavazos, the military post in the western part of the county.

  • Housing units: 165,094, of which 56.5 percent are lived in by their owners
  • Typical owned home, 2020 to 2024 survey: valued at $241,000
  • Typical monthly rent: $1,224
  • Veterans in the county: 48,220

Who sets the value of a Bell County property?

The Bell Central Appraisal District sets value, and the clerk only records the deed. The district keeps three public offices: Belton at 411 E. Central (254-939-5841), Killeen at 301 Priest Dr. (254-634-9752) and Temple at 205 E. Central (254-771-1108). All three open weekdays until 4:45 p.m., and one mailing box, P.O. Box 390 in Belton, serves them.

Its contact page sends deed and address-change questions to a mapping email, which matters after a sale: a recorded deed is what lets the district update ownership. Protests have their own address, and the district says protests will not be accepted at any other inbox.

Appraisals reflect ownership and condition on each January 1, with homestead notices mailed around April 1. A protest is due May 15 or 30 days from delivery of the notice, whichever falls later. Schools exempt $140,000 of a homestead's value, and owners aged 65 and up or with a disability get another $60,000.

How do Bell County records affect a house sale?

Whatever is recorded against the house shows up in the title search and can delay closing until it is paid or released. The Comptroller explains that each year's tax lien attaches January 1, and whoever owned the house on that day stays liable for that bill even after selling.

Foreclosure is visible in the same records. Trustees post a sale notice at the courthouse and file a copy with the clerk 21 or more days ahead, and the auction runs the first Tuesday of the month from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Bell County's schedule lists foreclosure postings at $2.00 when the trustee does it and $12.00 when the clerk posts.

Inherited houses add another layer. The State Law Library describes an affidavit of heirship as a sworn statement placed on file with the clerk, and nothing obliges a buyer or lender to rely on it. A deed that transfers property at death has to be recorded while the owner is alive, and a muniment of title order and will go to the clerk where the land lies.

  • Unpaid taxes, old mortgages and judgments need payoff letters before closing
  • Missing heirs or an unprobated will can stop a title company from insuring
  • A plat or survey mismatch is fixed by a corrective instrument that gets recorded

More questions about Bell County, TX Property Records

What will Bell County charge to file a single-page deed?

The charge is $10.00, split into a $5.00 filing fee and a $5.00 records management fee. Each added page with visible marks is $4.00, and names indexed beyond five are $0.25 each.

Is electronic filing open to homeowners in Bell County?

Only qualified filers can e-record. Local Government Code 195.003 limits it to groups such as attorneys, banks and title companies, working through vendors the clerk names. A homeowner mails or hand-delivers the notarized original in Belton.

When does the Bell County Clerk stop taking recordings each day?

Daily business transactions end at 4:30 p.m., and 4:15 p.m. applies on the last business day of the month, so month-end closings need documents delivered ahead of time.

Where can I order a certified Bell County deed copy?

Ask the County Clerk's recording desk at (254) 933-5171. The posted rate for a certified copy is $1.00 plus $1.00 per page, and a plain copy is $1.00 per page.

Which office handles questions about my Bell County valuation?

The Bell Central Appraisal District does. Its Belton line is 254-939-5841, Killeen is 254-634-9752 and Temple is 254-771-1108.

Clay County property records FAQ

Where do I search Clay County property records?

Start with the county clerk's office. We did not confirm an online search for this county.

Can I search Clay County property records online?

Not at this time, according to the clerk. The Clay County Clerk's page says deed records are digitized back to the 1960s and that property records are currently not available online. Plan to call or visit the clerk's office in Henrietta, and ask for the record by owner name, legal description or instrument number.

The clerk's page adds two limits owners should know. The clerk cannot give legal advice or services, and the clerk has no duty to search public records, citing Attorney General opinion WW-607. A title company or attorney does the searching.

Where is the Clay County Clerk's office and when is it open?

The office is in the Courthouse Annex at 214 N. Main Street, Henrietta, TX 76365, with a mailing address of P.O. Box 548. The phone is (940) 538-4631 and the fax is (940) 264-4160. Hours are Monday to Friday, 7:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., and the annex closes from noon to 1:00 p.m. every day.

  • The office closes for major holidays.
  • It may close for court hearings, training or bad weather, so call before a long drive.
  • Historic Commissioners' Court record books from the 1870s have been restored and are kept in the clerk's office.

What ID do I need to file a deed in Clay County?

A government photo ID. A notice posted by the clerk explains that Senate Bill 16, effective September 1, 2025, adds Local Government Code 191.010(b): the clerk must require photo ID from whoever presents a document for the real property records, must copy it, and must reject the filing if the person refuses.

The notice describes the law as a statewide deed fraud measure. It also tightens criminal penalties for real property theft and fraud, lets victims seek restitution and a no-fee judicial voiding of a fraudulent deed, and sets stronger standards for notaries. A seller who plans to mail a deed should ask the clerk how the ID rule applies to documents delivered by a title company.

What does the Clay County Clerk charge to record a deed?

The first page costs $25 in total, and each added page costs $4, based on the clerk's fee schedule effective September 1, 2025. Other recording lines from that schedule are below.

Clay County Clerk recording fees as printed in the schedule effective September 1, 2025
FilingFirst page, totalEach added page
Official Public Records (deeds, releases)$25.00$4.00
State tax lien or release$15.00$4.00
Federal tax lien or release$30.00$4.00
Plat inside city limits$85.00not listed
Plat outside city limits$325.00not listed

The $25 first-page figure is built from a $10 archive fee, a $5 recording fee and a $10 records management fee. Each name to be indexed beyond five adds $0.25.

What mistakes make the Clay County Clerk charge extra or refuse a deed?

Format errors raise the price or stop the filing, and the schedule lists them:

  • No grantee mailing address on a deed signed after December 31, 1981 brings a penalty equal to the greater of twice the filing fee or $25, on top of regular fees.
  • No clear heading at the top of the first page doubles the filing fee for that page.
  • Names not legibly typed or printed under each signature double the fee for that page.
  • Printed type must be no smaller than 8 point, per the schedule's citation of Local Government Code 191.007.
  • The deed needs original signatures and a proper acknowledgment under Property Code 12.001(b).

Copies cost $1.00 per page, certification is $5.00 per document, and a notice of trustee sale carries a $2.00 fee. A returned check costs $30.

Which state recording rules sit behind Clay County's fee schedule?

The Texas county clerk manual describes the clerk as the county recorder, with deed records filed in the county where the land lies. It lists the instruments a clerk records, among them general and special warranty deeds, quitclaim deeds, trustee's deeds, sheriff's deeds, tax deeds, deed of trust releases and powers of attorney. The manual also lets a commissioners court tell the clerk to waive real property recording fees for buyers using certain federal or state grant programs. Ask the Henrietta office whether that option has been adopted.

How do probate and heirs affect a Clay County house sale?

If an owner has died, a probate filing may be needed before the house can be sold. The County Clerk's fee schedule lists a base probate or guardianship filing at $360, and $418 when a citation is issued and posted by the sheriff. A will left for safekeeping with the clerk costs $16. The clerk's page also links a guardianship registration form and civil court cost instructions.

Ask the clerk or a Texas attorney which route fits a particular estate. County clerks cannot advise on that choice, as the clerk's page states plainly.

What does the Clay Appraisal District handle?

Value and exemptions, but not tax collection. The Clay County Appraisal District FAQ says it does not levy taxes, set rates or collect them, and that you must call the proper tax office for amounts. Its site, claycad.org, carries forms, an interactive map, protest hearing information and an oil and gas FAQ.

  • Homestead exemption: you must have owned and lived in the home on January 1, and it must be your principal residence. The district says the claim covers up to 20 acres of residential land.
  • Filing window: January 1 to April 30 of the tax year, with a late homestead claim allowed up to two years after taxes become delinquent.
  • Over 65: the claim can be filed up to one year after the 65th birthday, with proof of age.
  • Mobile homes can be set up as improvement-only accounts if you file a request for separate taxation with the title or a verified purchase contract.

The Comptroller calendar gives May 15, or the 30th day after notice is delivered when later, as the usual protest deadline. The CAD FAQ adds that a protest letter need not be on an official form.

What do the Census figures say about Clay County?

Clay is a thinly settled county. Census QuickFacts reports a July 2025 estimate of 10,764 people, up from 10,218 at the 2020 census, on 1,088.76 square miles. That works out to 9.4 people per square mile in 2020.

  • Housing units: 5,247, with only 8 building permits in 2025
  • Owner-occupied rate: 84.0%, across 4,289 households
  • Median owner-occupied home value: $171,500 for 2020 to 2024
  • Median gross rent: $811; median household income: $80,114
  • Residents 65 or older: 24.7%

With so few sales, a comparable house may be miles away. Ask a title company for recent recorded deed prices in your part of the county.

More questions about Clay County, TX Property Records

Are Clay County property records available online?

No. The Clay County Clerk's page says deed records are digitized back to the 1960s but that property records are currently not available online. Call (940) 538-4631 or visit the annex in Henrietta.

What are the hours of the Clay County Clerk?

Monday to Friday, 7:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., with the annex closed from noon to 1:00 p.m. daily. The office may close for hearings, training or bad weather.

Do I need a photo ID to record a deed in Clay County?

Yes. Under Local Government Code 191.010(b), added by Senate Bill 16 effective September 1, 2025, the clerk must require photo ID from the person presenting a real property document, copy it and reject the filing if the person refuses.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Clay County?

The clerk's schedule effective September 1, 2025 lists $25 for the first page and $4 for each added page. Missing grantee addresses, a missing heading or unreadable printed names add penalties.

Who collects property tax in Clay County?

Not the appraisal district. The Clay CAD says it does not collect taxes, so call the proper tax office for amounts. The appraisal district's site lists a separate Pay Taxes Online link for that purpose.
